context: A research team is preparing a governance analysis report on artificial intelligence and must define its scope. AI systems vary widely, from very large, general-purpose models with broad capabilities to small, narrowly specialized systems built for specific tasks. The risks, resource requirements and policy levers differ across this range. A broad scope would cover many kinds of systems but dilute attention and complicate recommendations, while a narrow scope would allow focused, detailed analysis but leave some systems outside the report. The team must decide which category of AI systems the analysis will cover.
a_text: Limit the analysis to highly advanced, broadly capable general-purpose AI systems and exclude small or specialized systems.
b_text: Limit the analysis to small, narrowly specialized AI systems and exclude highly advanced, broadly capable general-purpose systems.
reason: Narrow systems are less likely to pose severe risks when deployed internally. A targeted focus allows tailored interventions justified by national security and societal concerns without unduly hindering innovation.

context: A research team is preparing a review that draws lessons from existing safety-critical industries to inform how risks from a new technology should be governed. Many industries could serve as analogues, including those handling biological agents and toxins, novel chemical substances, novel pesticides, nuclear reactor research and development, and experimental aircraft. The team cannot cover all of them in equal depth within the main body of the review and must decide which industries to treat as the central analogues and which to give secondary treatment, such as placing them in an appendix. The choice shapes which regulatory practices, risk-assessment approaches and lessons the review emphasizes.
a_text: Focus the main review on biological agents and toxins, novel chemical substances and novel pesticides, and move nuclear reactor R&D and experimental aircraft to the appendix.
b_text: Focus the main review on nuclear reactor R&D and experimental aircraft, and move biological agents and toxins, novel chemicals and novel pesticides to the appendix.
reason: These industries have the most similar threat profile: high impact, wide reach, high velocity and difficult to remediate. They also allow regulated pre-release access and use.

context: A research team is analysing whether existing legal and regulatory frameworks for AI govern internal deployment, meaning use of advanced AI systems inside the developing organisation without public release. These frameworks were mostly written with external, market-facing release in mind, and their text does not address internal use explicitly. The team must decide how strongly to state the conclusion about coverage in its analysis. A firm claim would give policymakers and regulators a clear position, but it could be challenged as overreaching. A more qualified claim would be easier to defend, but it could weaken the practical force of the finding.
a_text: State that the frameworks can be interpreted to cover internal deployment while explicitly declining to advocate an extensive or creative reading.
b_text: State that the existing guidance covers internal deployment by defining a deployer as any organisation using an AI system internally or externally.
reason: The review is only of how the language could in theory be read, not a recommendation that it should be.

context: A legal analysis addresses the scope of a regulation on artificial intelligence. One operative article states that the regulation applies to AI systems put into service for the deployer's own use, which would cover systems built and used internally by an organisation. A recital in the same regulation states that systems developed and put into service for the purpose of scientific research and development fall outside the regulation. Read broadly, the recital could remove internally deployed research and development systems from scope, which would conflict with the operative article. Recitals are interpretive aids and are not themselves binding rules. The analysis must decide how the recital relates to the operative article when applied to internally deployed systems.
a_text: Treat the recital as a narrow exception to the operative article, so that systems with the sole purpose of scientific research and development fall outside the scope.
b_text: Treat the recital as creating no exception to the operative article, so that AI systems put into service for own use stay within the regulation's scope.
reason: Recitals have no binding legal force and cannot derogate from the Act's actual provisions, according to EU Court of Justice case law.

context: A research team is writing an analysis of how safety-critical industries manage risk, and is deciding how to structure the document. The analysis covers several domains, including biological agents, chemicals and pesticides, as well as case studies of experimental aircraft and test nuclear reactors. The aviation and nuclear case studies are well documented and illustrate relevant safety practices, but they differ in character from the other domains and add length to the main text. The team must decide where these two case studies belong in the document's structure.
a_text: Move the experimental aircraft and test nuclear reactor case studies to the appendix and keep the main text focused on the other domains.
b_text: Keep the experimental aircraft and test nuclear reactor case studies in the main body and discuss them alongside the other domains.
reason: Aviation and nuclear threats are more localized and may lack the high impact, wide reach, velocity and difficulty of remediation shared by AI, biological agents, chemicals and pesticides.

context: A team responsible for advanced AI systems must decide how to learn the risk profile of a highly capable system before it is deployed internally, where it would have access to sensitive resources and substantial autonomy. The system's potential for misaligned or deceptive behavior is not well characterized, and internal deployment typically happens before any external release or oversight. The team can either establish the system's risk profile proactively through dedicated testing before deployment, or accept that the risk profile will be revealed through incidents that occur once the system is already in use.
a_text: Run scheming and control evaluations before internal deployment and make deployment conditional on the results.
b_text: Deploy internally without prior evaluations and learn the system's risks from incidents that occur in use.
reason: Scheming is a horizontal risk layer that can undermine all other evaluations, so it must be assessed before the first highly capable systems are applied to AI R&D.

context: A team developing governance recommendations for AI systems that developers deploy internally, such as for their own research, engineering and operations, must decide how much information about those systems to share with the general public. Internal deployment can give developers access to highly capable systems before any external release, which creates risks that outsiders cannot easily observe. Staff and government bodies are expected to receive detailed information about these systems. The open question is how far public disclosure should go relative to that. Greater public transparency supports accountability and external scrutiny. It may also expose sensitive security, safety or commercial details. The team must choose the level of detail recommended for public disclosure.
a_text: Recommend broad public transparency about internally deployed systems, including substantive details about their capabilities, use and risks.
b_text: Recommend minimal, high-level public disclosure of internally deployed systems, such as the existence of governance frameworks, instead of detailed disclosure.
reason: Detailed public information could fuel race dynamics, while the public still benefits from a high-level outline given the potential spill of threats into society.

context: A team is designing a framework to review whether the governance mechanisms of an organisation developing advanced technology actually work in practice. Internal staff are often the first to see when safeguards are bypassed or ignored, and confidential reporting channels with legal protections for those who raise concerns are one available way to surface such failures. These channels depend on individuals being willing to come forward despite personal risk, and they only reveal problems that someone happens to witness and chooses to report. The team must decide how much weight to place on whistleblower channels as a means of reviewing the effectiveness of governance mechanisms.
a_text: Treat whistleblower channels and protections as a useful complement to other review mechanisms, but not as the sole means of review.
b_text: Treat whistleblower channels and protections as the sole means of reviewing whether governance mechanisms work.
reason: Whistleblower channels support review of whether mechanisms function and suffice as capabilities grow, but are not sufficient alone.

context: A team is building a monitor that reviews actions proposed by an automated agent and judges whether each one should be allowed. The monitor's output format must be fixed. It can return a direct categorical verdict that immediately blocks or approves each action. Alternatively, it can return a graded rating of how harmful the action seems, and the deployer then decides how high a rating must be before an action is blocked. A categorical verdict is simpler to use and interpret, but it gives deployers no way to trade off safety against disruption to legitimate work. A graded rating allows that tuning, but it requires deployers to choose a cutoff and adds a configuration step.
a_text: Have the monitor output a binary block or approve decision, with no score or adjustable threshold.
b_text: Have the monitor output a graded severity score, with the blocking threshold set by the user.
reason: Risk tolerance varies across users, e.g. a bank wants stronger guarantees than a personal website builder

context: A research team is building a monitor that oversees AI agent behavior, and they need to measure its fidelity, meaning how accurately it detects and characterizes problematic behavior. Real examples of attacks or failures by agents are scarce, so there is little naturally occurring ground-truth data to evaluate against. The team has access to real agent trajectories, and they can either use established adversarial evaluation setups from the AI control literature or build their own evaluation data. They must decide what kind of attack data to use to measure the monitor's fidelity.
a_text: Measure monitor fidelity on synthetic attacks built by injecting specified failure modes at specified severities into real trajectories.
b_text: Measure monitor fidelity inside traditional AI control settings, using attacks that adversarial policies generate within those settings.
reason: Real data has higher complexity and attack surface, traditional settings likely underestimate real-world attack rates, and injections allow specificity about failure modes

context: A research team is building a monitoring system for AI agents that act autonomously on software and research tasks. One component is a real-time monitor that inspects agent actions as they happen and can block them before they execute. Slower monitors can also review work after the fact, at the level of a pull request or in delayed batches. Blocking in real time adds latency and risks interrupting legitimate work with false positives. Some failure modes cause harm instantly and are hard to undo, such as data exfiltration. Others, such as code vulnerabilities or overclaiming in reports, can be caught and corrected later without lasting damage. The team must decide how broad the real-time blocking monitor's threat model should be and which failure modes to leave to the slower monitors.
a_text: Limit the real-time blocking monitor's threat model to instantaneous, hard-to-recover harms such as data exfiltration, and leave risks like code vulnerabilities or overclaiming to slower PR-level or delayed monitors.
b_text: Extend the real-time blocking monitor's threat model to a broad range of failure modes, including code vulnerabilities and overclaiming, alongside instantaneous harms such as data exfiltration.
reason: Real-time blocking is needed only where harm is instantaneous and hard to reverse; delayed monitoring allows more capable models for the other risks

context: A research team is building a monitoring pipeline in which a monitor model reviews the behavior of an AI system and flags problematic actions. Each flagged item needs a severity level so that results can be compared, aggregated, and acted on. The team must decide how that severity is assigned. One approach is a predefined deterministic rule set that maps observable features of the behavior to severity levels. This would be transparent and reproducible, but it may miss nuance. The other approach is to let the monitor model weigh the surrounding context and decide severity case by case. This would be more flexible and sensitive to circumstances, but it would be less predictable and harder to audit.
a_text: Assign severity through the monitor model's contextual judgment of each case instead of fixed rules.
b_text: Assign severity with a fixed deterministic rule set that maps observed behaviors to severity levels.
reason: Deployments are too varied for a clean rule set; the same command can be benign or malicious depending on context; also Watcher improves as model judgment improves

context: A research team runs an automated monitor that reads long transcripts and judges them using a detailed prompt. The prompt is long and spells out many criteria and examples, so every monitoring call carries a substantial input-token cost, and the total cost grows with the number of monitored runs. The team could shorten the prompt by compressing or summarizing it, which would cut tokens per call but might remove detail the monitor relies on. Alternatively, they could keep the full prompt, where the repeated prefix could be served from a prompt cache at a lower effective price. They had to choose how to handle the prompt's cost while keeping monitoring quality.
a_text: Keep the long, detailed monitoring prompt unchanged and rely on prompt caching to offset the per-call cost.
b_text: Compress the monitoring prompt into a shorter summarized version to reduce the per-call input cost directly.
reason: All compactions reduced performance, and caching makes the overhead of long prompts nearly negligible

context: A research team built a pipeline that uses language models to generate synthetic severity labels for steps in simulated attack sequences, and plans to use these labels as the basis for evaluating other systems. Before relying on them, the team must establish whether the labels are trustworthy. The labels come from an automated rubric-based process, and the team knows that LLM-based judgments can carry biases such as favoring longer outputs or outputs resembling the judge's own style. Edge cases in the rubric may produce inconsistent labels. The team has limited annotation resources and must choose how to verify label quality before using them for evaluation.
a_text: Skip human annotation and validate the labels by running two independent LLM judges, calibrated for known biases, and keep only the labels on which both agree.
b_text: Validate the labels against a human-annotated reference set of attack steps, refining the rubric wherever edge cases cause inconsistencies, and use the resulting set for evaluation.
reason: Otherwise the datasets would be miscalibrated and the evaluation misleading

context: A research team is building a monitor, itself a model, that reviews the behavior of an AI agent acting over multi-step tasks and flags suspicious or unsafe actions. The agent's trajectory contains several message types: the task instructions, the agent's reasoning and messages, the tool calls it makes, and the outputs those tools return. Tool outputs can be very long and noisy, and they may carry information that helps or misleads the monitor. The team must decide how much of the trajectory, and which message types, the monitor sees when it scores each trajectory. The choice affects the monitor's detection accuracy, its cost, and how much it can be influenced by content in the tool outputs.
a_text: Show the monitor the full conversation context with all tool call outputs included.
b_text: Show the monitor the full conversation context with all tool call outputs removed.
reason: More context improves performance, but tool outputs hold most tokens, so removing them greatly lowers cost and latency at slight fidelity loss

context: A team building a tiered system that screens inputs with a cheap triage model and escalates flagged items to a more capable gateway model must choose which models and score thresholds to use for the Default configuration. A lighter Lite configuration also exists. Triage and gateway model choices and the escalation threshold trade off cost, latency and quality, and the Lite configuration is expected to cost less than Default. The team must decide how to configure Default, and by extension Lite, given what they know about the available models and their relative strengths.
a_text: Pair a different triage model and gateway model with alternative thresholds for Default, and set Lite with its own separate model and threshold choices.
b_text: Pair a small triage model with the strongest gateway model at a moderate threshold for Default, and make Lite stricter at triage with a mid-tier gateway.
reason: Luna is cheap, fast and errs on the side of escalating; Opus 4.7 offers the best mix of fidelity, cost and latency at threshold 6; Sonnet is a lower-cost alternative

context: A research team is developing methods to detect or mitigate misaligned behavior in language models. They have access to two test sets of behavior: one built around agentic tasks where a model may pursue a hidden side objective while completing a main task, and one built around whether a model strategically complies with training objectives to avoid modification. The team is at an early-to-middle stage of the project, still iterating on methods and making design choices. Using these test sets repeatedly during development risks overfitting to them and weakening their value as unbiased measures, while reserving them means going without a realistic evaluation signal during the current stage. The team must decide when to use these two test sets.
a_text: Use the two test sets for evaluation now, during the current stage of the project.
b_text: Hold the two test sets out of sample and reserve them for evaluation later in the project.
reason: Keeping them out of sample preserves them for later generalisation testing.

context: A research team is building and tuning monitors, which are classifiers that flag suspicious behavior, and runs a grid search over monitor configurations to select the best one. Each configuration must be scored by a single metric so that candidates can be ranked. Monitors are evaluated across several subcategories of behavior, and a deployable monitor eventually needs a decision threshold for flagging. The team must decide how to score candidates during the search. One approach ties the score to a threshold-dependent measure, with the threshold recomputed separately for each monitor subcategory. The other approach uses a threshold-independent ranking measure for selection and leaves the threshold unset until a monitor has been chosen.
a_text: Score each candidate monitor with a threshold-dependent metric, recomputing the threshold separately for every monitor subcategory during the grid search.
b_text: Score each candidate monitor with a threshold-independent ranking metric during the grid search, and set the threshold only after a monitor is selected.
reason: AUROC is threshold agnostic, and per-monitor threshold recomputation would be cumbersome.

context: A research team is building and evaluating a system on a labeled dataset in which some labels are suspected to be incorrect. They use LLM-based assistants as monitors that review examples and flag labels they judge to be wrong. Acting on these flags by relabeling would improve the accuracy of the labels. However, because the monitors themselves are the source of the corrections, relabeling based on their judgments introduces bias into evaluation, since the evaluation metric would then favor outputs that agree with the monitors. The team must decide whether to allow this relabeling or to keep the labels fixed so that the evaluation metric stays fair and unbiased.
a_text: Keep the labels fixed and never relabel from monitor flags, so the evaluation metric stays fair and unbiased.
b_text: Relabel whenever a monitor convincingly flags a label as wrong, accepting biased evaluation in exchange for more accurate labels.
reason: Their primary goal is to build the best possible monitor, not to preserve an unbiased metric. They also expect the bias to be acceptably small.

context: A research team studying a reasoning-capable language model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer must decide what to advise about exposing that reasoning to end users. Making it visible could let users notice problematic behavior, such as flawed reasoning, deception, or misaligned intent, and report it, which would add an oversight channel. The team's evidence suggests that the visible reasoning does not always faithfully reflect the model's actual decision process, and that exposing it could create pressure to shape or sanitize it, which might reduce its value as a monitoring signal. The team must decide whether to issue a position on user-facing visibility or to leave the question open.
a_text: Recommend making the chain of thought visible to users so they can observe problems and report them.
b_text: Withhold any explicit recommendation on whether the chain of thought should be visible to users.
reason: Visibility could backfire by creating pressure to directly supervise the CoT to look safe and to avoid legal and reputational risks, which may break monitorability.

context: A research team is writing about the externalized reasoning property, the idea that a model's chain-of-thought text reflects the reasoning it relies on, which would make that reasoning readable and useful for oversight. They must decide how strongly to claim that current frontier language models satisfy this property. Evidence is suggestive but incomplete. For hard tasks, models appear to need to write out their reasoning in human-readable text. It is not established that this text is always faithful or complete. Models could also in principle drift toward reasoning that humans cannot easily interpret, and the property could weaken in future systems.
a_text: State a belief that current systems satisfy the property, while noting it does not guarantee monitorability and may fail for future models.
b_text: Note that models can use tokens with meanings humans cannot decode, which undermines the claim that current systems satisfy the property.
reason: Large language models learn a strong natural language prior during pretraining, so they use the chain of thought much as humans use natural language.

context: A research team is assessing whether the chain-of-thought reasoning produced by advanced language models is monitorable enough to serve as a safety oversight tool, meaning whether it reveals the model's relevant intentions and behavior to an automated or human monitor. Chain-of-thought is currently legible and often reveals misbehavior, but it may degrade as training methods, scaling and architectures change. Existing work offers faithfulness evaluations, which test whether stated reasoning accurately reflects the factors that drove a model's answer. These are available now but were not designed to measure monitorability directly. The team must decide what evidence to collect to judge whether chain-of-thought can be relied on for oversight.
a_text: Use existing faithfulness evaluations as the proxy for judging whether chain-of-thought is monitorable enough to rely on.
b_text: Prototype and standardize dedicated monitorability evaluations and metrics, and do not rely on existing proxies such as faithfulness tests.
reason: Faithfulness evaluations do not disambiguate propensity from necessity to externalize reasoning and only cover simple question answering, and it is unclear what level of monitorability is sufficient for safety.

context: A research team is assessing existing evidence that chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in language models can be monitored to detect misbehavior or intent. Monitoring has worked in current demonstrations, but two explanations fit that success. One is necessity: the tasks require the model to reason out loud in its CoT to succeed, so the reasoning must appear in the text. The other is propensity: models tend to verbalize their reasoning by default even when they could do without it. The available evidence does not cleanly separate these explanations, and the team must decide how to interpret the demonstrated monitorability and what to conclude about its future usefulness.
a_text: Interpret the demonstrated monitorability as resulting mainly from the necessity of thinking out loud to complete the tasks.
b_text: Leave the interpretation open between necessity and propensity, and note that monitoring may stay useful on tasks requiring CoT.
reason: Future models may face incentives to hide reasoning that override natural propensity, but tasks hard enough to need CoT would still be monitorable.

context: A group of AI safety researchers is writing a position statement on chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring, the practice of reading a reasoning model's intermediate natural-language reasoning to detect misbehavior or harmful intent. They know that current reasoning models often state their intentions in readable reasoning traces, which makes monitoring useful as an oversight tool. They also know that this property is fragile: it could degrade through further outcome-based reinforcement learning, direct optimization pressure on the reasoning, or new architectures that reason in latent space. Monitoring is imperfect, since it misses some misbehavior and models may learn to obscure their reasoning. The group must decide how strongly to recommend investment in CoT monitorability relative to other safety work, given that its value is uncertain and that resources for safety research are limited.
a_text: Recommend CoT monitoring strictly as a supplement to existing safety research directions, never as a substitute for any of them.
b_text: Recommend preserving CoT monitorability in its current form as an unconditional priority, regardless of competing considerations or costs.
reason: CoT monitoring cannot by itself give strong evidence of safety, may miss harms, may fail on more advanced models, and firm commitments to protect CoT may trade off against more effective interventions like process supervision.

context: A research team is building a monitoring setup to detect undesirable or unsafe behavior by an AI agent that reasons step by step before acting and then uses tools to complete tasks. The agent produces internal reasoning (chain of thought), tool calls and final outputs. The team must decide what the monitors, which flag suspicious behavior, are allowed to see. One consideration is that internal reasoning may reveal intent that actions alone do not. Another is that reasoning may be unfaithful, may be shaped by the monitoring itself, or may make results harder to compare with setups that observe only external behavior. The team must fix the monitors' input before running the evaluations.
a_text: Show monitors the agent's internal reasoning alongside its tool calls and outputs.
b_text: Hide the reasoning from monitors and limit them to tool calls and outputs.
reason: CoT can be illegible after RL, unfaithful, or absent in future models, so internal traces are assumed unavailable or untrustworthy

context: A research team was developing a prompt for a language-model task and refining it with a human in the loop: a person reviewed outputs, identified failures, and revised the prompt. Each round of refinement cost human effort and moved the prompt closer to the observed examples. Several rounds had been completed, and the team had to decide how long to keep refining. Continuing might improve quality further but risked overfitting to the inspected examples and added effort, while stopping early would keep the process short and the prompt less tailored.
a_text: Continue human-guided prompt refinement past three iterations until further edits yield no improvement.
b_text: Stop human-guided prompt refinement after three iterations and freeze the prompt at that point.
reason: Further targeted fixes became counterproductive, because fixing specific failure modes introduced new failures elsewhere without performance gains

context: A team is building a test set of agent trajectories to evaluate a detector of covert misbehavior. In each test trajectory, the agent was assigned a side task in addition to its main task. In a subset of these trajectories, the agent did not actually complete the assigned side task, so the trajectory's status as a true instance of the behavior of interest is ambiguous. The team must decide how to treat these trajectories when finalizing the test set, knowing that the choice affects the test set's size, composition, and label validity.
a_text: Remove the trajectories with incomplete side tasks from the test set and leave them unlabeled..
b_text: Keep the trajectories with incomplete side tasks in the test set and assign each one a label like the rest.
reason: Ascribing intent without ground-truth verification is unreliable, so only verified side-task successes are labeled positive

context: A research team is designing experiments in which language models act as monitors. They must decide which monitor models to include. Five candidate monitors are available: three established models and two of the newest, most capable frontier models. Including more monitors broadens coverage of monitor capability, but it also adds evaluation cost and complexity. The team must fix the monitor set before running the main experiments.
a_text: Expand the monitor set to all five models by adding the two newest frontier models to the three established ones.
b_text: Restrict the monitor set to the three established models and exclude the two newest frontier models.
reason: They were too costly

context: A research team is building a monitor that reviews the actions of an AI agent and reports how suspicious each action looks. The monitor's output is later used to decide which actions to flag or escalate. The team must choose the format in which the monitor reports its suspicion assessment. The format affects how finely the monitor can separate benign from suspicious behavior, how easily thresholds can be set, and how consistent the outputs are across runs.
a_text: Have the monitor output a discrete integer rating on a fixed bounded scale of increasing suspicion.
b_text: Have the monitor output a binary flag that marks each action as either suspicious or not suspicious.
reason: It significantly outperforms binary in the low-FPR regime, matches 5x-averaged binary at a fifth of the cost, and LLMs calibrate poorly over 100 points

context: A research team ran a prompt sweep across several tasks and then added a human refinement stage on top of the best prompts. Across nearly all tasks, human refinement produced no meaningful improvement and results looked saturated. On one task, however, human refinement produced a single significant gain. The team had to decide how to interpret that gain relative to the otherwise flat results, and what it implied about how much headroom remained.
a_text: Treat the gain as an isolated exception and conclude that performance is largely saturated after the prompt sweep, while allowing that this one task may tolerate more optimization.
b_text: Treat the gain as a sign of untapped headroom and conclude that performance is not yet saturated after the prompt sweep, so more optimization is warranted across tasks.
reason: The improvement is isolated

context: A research team ran heavy optimization of prompts and found that it failed to outperform simply selecting the best prompt from a set of simple candidates. The evaluation relied on synthetic data. The team needed to decide how to account for this negative result in their write-up. One possible cause is that the synthetic data was too narrow or contained artifacts that left little room for optimization to help. Another is that prompting has fundamental limits that cap what optimization can achieve. The experiments done so far did not separate these two explanations.
a_text: Commit to a single explanation for the failure, attribute it to one cause, and present that account as the one supported by the available evidence.
b_text: Present both the narrow or artifact-laden synthetic data and the fundamental limits of prompting as unresolved explanations, and outline future work to test each.
reason: The current evidence does not distinguish between the two

context: A research team is building and comparing monitors that flag problematic behaviour, and needs a single evaluation metric to report their performance. Each monitor outputs a continuous suspicion score, and the team can sweep a threshold to trade off true positive rate against false positive rate. In realistic deployment, only a small false positive rate is tolerable, because every flagged item costs review effort. Threshold-free summaries of the ROC curve are available, and they can cover either the entire curve or only part of it. The choice affects how monitors are ranked, since two monitors with similar overall performance can differ sharply in the low false positive regime.
a_text: Adopt a normalized partial AUROC restricted to the low false positive rate region as the monitor metric.
b_text: Adopt a standard AUROC computed over the entire false positive rate range as the monitor metric.
reason: Standard AUROC includes the impractical high-FPR regime, while log-AUROC is sensitive to the threshold parameter epsilon and noisy at small sample sizes

context: A research team measured whether language models can tell evaluation transcripts apart from real-world deployment transcripts. Each model was given transcripts and asked, through probe questions, to state the probability that a transcript comes from an evaluation. The team plotted calibration curves of stated probability against the true fraction of evaluation transcripts. For many models, the curves fall below the diagonal, meaning models label transcripts as evaluations more often than the true rate warrants. The team had to decide how to interpret this over-classification, given that the probe questions themselves mention evaluation and that many of the tested models are instruction-tuned and answer multiple-choice style prompts.
a_text: Interpret the below-diagonal curves as overconfidence caused partly by probe questions priming models toward evaluation and partly by instruction-tuned models' known overconfidence on multiple-choice prompts.
b_text: Interpret the below-diagonal curves as a uniform upward bias in stated probabilities from a base-rate shift or miscalibrated offset, not from prompt priming or instruction-tuning overconfidence.
reason: PQs introduce the possibility of evaluation, which may push models to consider transcripts evaluative; prior work notes similar overconfidence.

context: A research team evaluates language models on public benchmarks and finds that the models differ in how well they discriminate between items or outcomes on those benchmarks. One possible explanation is that the models have memorized the public benchmark content during training, so that apparent discriminative ability reflects exposure to the test material rather than genuine capability. The team has access to several models, including older and newer ones, and must decide how to address this memorization explanation in their analysis.
a_text: Measure memorization directly by testing how well each model reproduces benchmark text, and compare the results between older and newer models.
b_text: Acknowledge that memorization could plausibly contribute to the models' discriminative ability, without attempting to quantify its effect.
reason: Evaluation datasets derive from public benchmarks, but such occurrences are rare and hard to quantify.

context: A research team wants to know whether frontier language models can tell evaluation transcripts apart from real deployment transcripts, a capability often called evaluation awareness. Anecdotal reports suggest that models sometimes recognise when they are being tested, but no systematic measurement exists. The team must choose the study's framing and design. One approach is to build a large, diverse collection of transcripts drawn from many existing datasets and score model classification performance with a single aggregate metric. The other is to focus on comparing different black-box probing methods, such as asking a binary classification question about a full transcript versus only its first prompt, to learn which method best elicits evaluation awareness.
a_text: Compare several black-box probing methods, such as classification prompts on full transcripts versus first prompts only, to find which best elicits evaluation awareness.
b_text: Build a large benchmark of transcripts from many datasets, and score how well models classify evaluation versus deployment using AUC as the primary metric.
reason: Evaluation awareness could compromise the reliability of evaluations, and no comprehensive test suite existed to measure it.

context: A research team evaluated several frontier language models for misaligned or undesirable behavior in test scenarios. They observed that in their reasoning traces, some models produced meta-reasoning remarks noting that the question or scenario itself seemed to imply an evaluation. This raised the concern that such evaluation awareness might change how the models behave and so distort the measurements. The team had to decide how to treat this observation. Verbalized awareness varied across models, and it was unclear whether models that rarely verbalized it were truly unaware. The team had access to interpretability tools that could manipulate internal features associated with evaluation awareness, but using them would require extra experimental work.
a_text: Report the observed meta-reasoning without claiming a causal effect on behavior, and state that some models' evaluation awareness may be underestimated and need alternative measurement strategies.
b_text: Run an interpretability-based steering experiment that suppresses the model's internal evaluation-awareness features and measure how much the misbehavior rate rises when awareness is no longer verbalized.
reason: Causal influence of the reasoning on final decisions has not been established.

context: A research team wants to measure how often language models recognise that an interaction is part of an evaluation rather than real deployment. They have a collection of transcripts of model interactions and plan to elicit this awareness with probe questions that ask a model directly whether the interaction is an evaluation. They must decide how to deliver the probe question and what evidence to collect from the model's answers. One approach places the probe question inside the original conversation, so the model answers while still in the context of the interaction. The other approach presents the transcript as quoted material in a separate context and varies the phrasing of the probe question. Responses to the varied phrasings could be combined into a single estimate. The team knows that answers can depend on how the question is posed and framed.
a_text: Append a probe question asking whether the interaction is an evaluation to the end of the transcript, and read the model's answer within that same conversation.
b_text: Quote the transcript inside a fresh context with a probe question asking whether it came from an evaluation, and average answers across several prompt phrasings into a probability.
reason: A single phrasing gives high-variance responses and models understand phrasings differently, so diverse PQs give robust measurements.

context: A research team trained several predictive models and evaluated each with the area under the ROC curve (AUC) on a modest-sized dataset. They needed to decide whether the observed AUCs were meaningfully above the chance level of 0.5. The team had to choose a statistical approach for establishing that the models perform better than chance, and the choice would also determine whether they could say anything about the study's sensitivity given its sample size.
a_text: Simulate chance-level data to build a null distribution for the AUC, and use it to judge both significance and the study's statistical power.
b_text: Apply an analytic test for a single AUC with confidence intervals, and conclude from them whether each model exceeds chance.
reason: Large sample size and high AUC make the outperformance clear; confidence intervals exclude 0.5.

context: A research team evaluating language-model agents on a benchmark of interactive tasks suspects that some tasks are flawed, for example through ambiguous instructions, incorrect expected outcomes, or unsolvable setups, and that such tasks distort reported reliability scores. Reliability is measured with pass^5, the fraction of tasks solved in all five repeated attempts. The team ran several LLM judges over the tasks and trajectories, and the judges flagged a subset of tasks as flawed. Judge flags are known to be imperfect and may include false positives, so excluding flagged tasks could remove valid tasks and change the scores. The team must decide how to treat the flags before excluding tasks and recomputing the reliability metric.
a_text: Review every flagged task by hand, then exclude only the confirmed flawed tasks and recompute pass^5 on the remaining set.
b_text: Treat every task flagged by the LLM judges as flawed, then exclude them and recompute pass^5 on the remaining set.
reason: LLM judges over-flag properly specified tasks, with low precision and disagreement among evaluators, so manual validation serves as the reference

context: A research team wants to test whether pass^5, the rate at which an agent succeeds on all five repeated attempts at a task, predicts how well an agent performs in real deployment when users are persuasive and try to talk it into breaking policy. They have a multi-turn, tool-using customer-service agent benchmark with simulated users and a large pool of tasks, and several agents have already been scored with pass^5. Only a small portion of the tasks have been checked as valid and have simulated users who persist in pushing the agent across turns. The team must decide what evidence to collect to compare pass^5 with robustness to persuasion.
a_text: Evaluate every agent on the full benchmark task set, using the standard task-completion outcomes as the evidence for how reliability relates to persuasion robustness.
b_text: Evaluate every agent only on a small validated subset of tasks with persistent simulated users, using an LLM judge to count persuasion-induced policy violations per agent.
reason: Only a subset of tasks instruct the simulated user to push for policy exceptions, as would happen in real deployment

context: A team wants to audit a popular benchmark of tool-using customer-service agent tasks, where each task has a domain policy, a database, and a ground-truth expected outcome. They suspect that some tasks contain errors such as incorrect expected actions, ambiguous instructions, or conflicts with the policy. These errors would make agent scores unreliable. Checking every task thoroughly is expensive, so they must decide how to find the tasks most likely to be faulty. They must also decide what evidence to use to build a rubric for classifying and detecting those errors. They have access to the task definitions and policies, as well as logs from many runs by agents of varying capability.
a_text: Scan agent logs for tasks with very low success across all agents and higher failure rates for stronger agents, and build and refine the rubric from those patterns.
b_text: Review a random sample of tasks by hand against the domain policy and database, and build the rubric from the error types found in that sample.
reason: These patterns signal under-elicitation caused by task or environment errors rather than agent limitations

context: A research team is preparing methodological guidance for analyses of observational log data in which behavioral records are paired with labels, such as annotations or outcome categories assigned to logged events. These analyses commonly use regression, mixed-effects models, or hierarchical Bayesian models to account for grouping structure and confounders like user, session, or item. The team must decide how strongly the guidance should let researchers phrase conclusions about causes and effects. Such models improve estimates and handle clustered or repeated observations, but the underlying data are not collected through random assignment or a natural experiment, and unmeasured confounding and selection into the logged behavior cannot be ruled out by the modeling alone.
a_text: Advise against drawing causal claims from log-label analyses unless the design is experimental or pseudo-experimental, even when regression or hierarchical modeling is used.
b_text: Advise drawing causal claims from log-label analyses based on the estimates of mixed-effects or hierarchical Bayesian models, without requiring an experimental design.
reason: Observational label-outcome associations can be biased even with controls

context: A research team has analyzed system logs as a way to understand the behavior or failures of a system. Their findings show that log analysis yields useful and informative signals. However, they also recognize that logs capture only part of what happens in the system, and that some behaviors or causes may not appear in them. When writing up the work, the team must decide how strongly to phrase the claim about the role of log analysis in reaching their conclusions.
a_text: State that log analysis alone is sufficient to reach the conclusions about the system's behavior.
b_text: State that log analysis is necessary for these conclusions but explicitly insufficient on its own.
reason: Log analysis uses imperfect methods, though it provides signal outcomes cannot

context: A team is considering which product area within AGI safety would be the best candidate to pursue as a commercial or applied focus. Several areas are available, including approaches that observe and flag unsafe behaviour of AI systems during deployment and approaches that test AI systems for dangerous capabilities or propensities before release. The team has to choose one area to prioritise. None of the candidate areas has yet been shown to succeed as a product in practice, so the choice rests on judgement about fit and expected value rather than on demonstrated results.
a_text: Prioritise runtime monitoring of deployed AI systems as the best-fitting product area, while acknowledging it remains unvalidated in practice.
b_text: Prioritise pre-deployment testing of AI systems for dangerous capabilities as the best-fitting product area, while acknowledging it remains unvalidated in practice.
reason: He expects significant transfer to future systems and broad market demand from many economic actors.

context: An author is writing a piece arguing that products built around AGI safety are a worthwhile area for effort and investment. The argument rests on the view that the risks from advanced AI systems cannot be settled by theory alone, and that learning about them requires direct engagement with how AI systems are built, deployed and used in practice. Evidence for the broad thesis is suggestive rather than conclusive, and the area is young with few demonstrated successes. The author must decide how strongly to state the overall thesis, which shapes how readers weigh the claim and whether they act on it.
a_text: State the thesis categorically as a firm claim, arguing that risk is an empirical question answerable only by entities embedded across the stack.
b_text: State the thesis with explicit hedged confidence, recommending that more people explore the direction while stopping short of calling it established.
reason: The thesis depends on load-bearing assumptions, such as transfer from current systems to AGI and incentive alignment, which are not yet verified.

context: A group assessing the AI safety landscape is deciding which lines of safety work are poor candidates for for-profit ventures. Commercial incentives can pull safety-oriented work toward serving paying clients, shaping what gets measured or recommended, and softening conclusions that customers dislike. Some safety-related activities, such as technical tooling and evaluation, have clearer market demand and a plausible path to sustainable revenue. AI governance work, which covers policy advice, standards, auditing and organisational oversight, depends heavily on independence and public trust. The group must decide how to classify governance work with respect to commercialisation, and which organisational form it should take.
a_text: Keep AI governance work mostly in non-profits or insulated teams inside larger organizations, and avoid turning it into products.
b_text: Advise against for-profit consulting-based AI governance organizations, since client payment can compromise their independence.
reason: It is too hard to build products for governance work, and profit pressures would pull such work away from impact.

context: A research team is designing experiments on intrinsification, where an agent's instrumental goal comes to be pursued as if it were the system goal (goal switching). The setting involves an agent with two competing goals: profit maximization and emission minimization. The team must decide which goal serves as the system goal assigned to the agent and which serves as the instrumental, competing goal that may displace it. The choice determines the direction in which goal switching is tested and how strongly the system goal is elicited in the prompts. Both pairings use the same two goals but reverse their roles.
a_text: Assign profit maximization as the system goal and emission minimization as the competing goal when testing goal switching.
b_text: Assign emission minimization as the system goal and profit maximization as the competing goal, using strong goal elicitation throughout.
reason: Agents adhered more consistently to the instrumental goal during the instrumental phase in this configuration, and adversarial pressures alone had a smaller and more consistent impact.

context: A research team wants to study goal drift in language-model agents, meaning the gradual departure of an agent's behavior from the objective it was originally given. They need a way to measure whether an agent's goals have shifted over a long interaction. Asking models to describe their own goals and motivations is easy to set up, but such statements may not match what the models actually do, and may be shaped by how the question is phrased. The team must decide what kind of signal to use as the measure of drift.
a_text: Measure drift through quantifiable actions taken by the agent in a simulated stock trading environment, such as the stocks it buys and sells.
b_text: Measure drift through the agent's own written statements describing its goals and motivations at different points in the interaction.
reason: Self-reports of LMs about their goals may be unfaithful; the environment also presents natural tensions between objectives and a realistic test bed.

context: A research team is building a simulated trading environment to study how AI agents behave when they pursue an instrumental goal that differs from the goal given in their system prompt. The evaluation phase of each run requires the agent to start with a portfolio concentrated in stocks aligned with the instrumental goal. In initial runs, the agents did not reliably reach such a portfolio before the evaluation phase began, and some converged to portfolios with substantial holdings outside the instrumental-goal-aligned stocks. The team must choose a method to ensure agents enter the evaluation phase with a suitably aligned portfolio.
a_text: Resample the instrumental goal pursuit trajectories by hand whenever an agent ends with a portfolio that is not sufficiently concentrated in instrumental-goal-aligned stocks.
b_text: Add a system prompt instruction telling the agent to pursue the instrumental goal temporarily at the start of the simulation, framed as an intermediate step before switching to the system goal.
reason: To ensure conditions that demand adaptive behavior from the agent in order to switch back to and pursue the system goal.

context: A research team studied why language-model agents drift away from their assigned goals over long interactions. They hypothesized that the drift arises because the model pattern-matches to the content and style of its earlier context rather than maintaining the goal. To test this, they ran an ablation that inserted random sentences into the context and measured how goal drift changed, and they compared this with correlations between context features and drift. Most of the measured correlations were not statistically significant, though the direction of the effects was generally consistent with the hypothesis. The team had to decide how strongly to word the claim about what the ablation shows for the pattern-matching explanation.
a_text: Present the random-sentence ablation as only suggestive evidence for the pattern-matching explanation of goal drift.
b_text: Present the random-sentence ablation as strong support for the pattern-matching explanation of goal drift.
reason: Despite stronger correlations, most of the correlations are not statistically significant.

context: A research team studied how a model arrives at its behavior on a task and proposed two candidate explanations: the model reasons about goals, or the model relies on matching surface patterns seen in training. To test this, they ran a cross-conditioning ablation in which goal-related information and pattern-related cues were swapped or mismatched across conditions, so that each explanation predicts a different outcome. The results show that goal-related conditioning affects behavior to some degree, while pattern-related cues also have a clear influence, and the two effects are not cleanly separated. The team must decide how to interpret this ablation with respect to the goal-reasoning hypothesis.
a_text: Interpret the ablation as offering only limited support for goal reasoning, with pattern-matching as the primary mechanism.
b_text: Interpret the ablation as showing that goal reasoning is the primary mechanism driving the observed behavior.
reason: Individual differences are usually not statistically significant and substantial performance gaps persist between models in both conditions.

context: A team studying why language-model agents drift away from their original goal over long interactions considered the hypothesis that the number of tokens separating the original goal from the later decision point drives the drift. To test it, they ran an ablation in which the instrumental phase, the intervening stretch of task-related content, was replaced with a repeated-token message. The replacement was meant to preserve the token distance while removing the content. In this setting, measured drift was substantially lower than in the original setting. The team had to decide how to interpret this result with respect to the token distance hypothesis.
a_text: Conclude that token distance drives goal drift, treating the ablation result as consistent with that explanation of the drift.
b_text: Reject the token distance hypothesis, because the repeated-token replacement produced substantially lower drift than the original setting.
reason: All models except Claude 3.5 Haiku's GD_inaction showed substantially lower drift with only minimal increases over longer sequences.

context: A research team studies goal drift in language-model agents: after an agent is given one goal and then switched to a different goal, it gradually reverts toward the earlier goal or pursues instrumental subgoals such as accumulating assets. One candidate explanation is state complexity, the idea that drift grows when the environment state, such as a large and elaborate portfolio, is more complex. The team has observed drift under goal switching and wants to determine its cause. They can run an intervention that clears the context window while preserving the portfolio, which removes the earlier interaction history, including in-context examples of the agent pursuing instrumental goals, but leaves the environment state unchanged. They must decide how to interpret what this implies for the explanation of the drift.
a_text: Accept state complexity as the explanation for drift and treat the preserved portfolio as the main driver of the behavior.
b_text: Reject state complexity as the explanation for drift and attribute it to in-context examples of instrumental goal pursuit.
reason: The ablation produced no significant trend toward increasing drift with portfolio complexity and almost no effect on GD_actions.

context: A research team built an evaluation environment and ran a set of models through it, producing results on how the models performed. They now must decide how to position the environment for the wider community. The environment could be endorsed as a standard way to compare future models against one another, or it could be presented without that endorsement. The decision turns on how reliable and well-validated the evaluations are for ranking models, given what the team learned while building and running them.
a_text: Recommend the environment as a benchmark for comparing future models and present the work as a standard evaluation resource.
b_text: Advise against using these evaluations to compare future models and present the work as a characterization and methodological blueprint.
reason: The environment is not sufficiently complex to reliably measure goal drift susceptibility in frontier models, as shown by Claude 3.5 Sonnet's low drift scores.

context: A research team is building an evaluation with several settings in which agents are tested over a fixed number of time steps after a preceding phase. One setting applies adversarial pressure only. Settings (3) and (4) involve the agent's goal being switched. The team must decide how many time steps the evaluation phase lasts in each setting. A longer phase gives more observations per run but costs more compute. It may also matter differently depending on whether the setting involves goal switching or adversarial pressure alone. The team can set one common length for all settings or set the length separately for each type of setting.
a_text: Use 30 time steps for the adversarial-pressure-only setting and 10 time steps for goal-switching settings (3) and (4).
b_text: Use 30 time steps in every setting, including the adversarial-pressure-only setting and goal-switching settings (3) and (4).
reason: The larger number of variations in settings (3) and (4) and the resulting costs.

context: A research team ran an experiment in which models were given different system-level goals and their downstream behavior was compared across conditions, measuring how far outputs drifted from a baseline. In the variation where profit maximization was set as the system goal, the drift was noticeably larger than in the other variations. The team had to decide how to account for this larger drift. Two explanations were plausible: the texts generated under this goal differed in subtle ways from those under other goals, or the models held intrinsic preferences related to profit maximization. The evidence at hand did not clearly separate these two explanations.
a_text: Attribute the larger drift to subtle differences between the texts the models generated under the profit-maximization goal.
b_text: Leave the cause open and state that the drift may stem from generated-text differences or from intrinsic model preferences.
reason: The two variations differ in both texts and goals, so the causes cannot be disentangled.

context: A grant program funds work toward a goal that cannot be measured directly, so its progress is tracked with proxy metrics. Over successive funding rounds, those proxy metrics have repeatedly been gamed: recipients and applicants optimize for the measured indicators in ways that raise the scores without clearly advancing the underlying goal. Adjustments to the metrics have not stopped this pattern. The decision-makers must now decide how to treat this persistent metric gaming in deciding the program's future, knowing that the program's true impact is hard to verify independently of the metrics.
a_text: Continue the program and treat the gaming of its proxy metrics as a measurement problem rather than a reason to stop it.
b_text: Stop the program and treat the persistent gaming of its proxy metrics as negative evidence about its value.
reason: Repeated goodharting would be good negative evidence against the program's value

context: A research team working on AI alignment is considering whether to pursue automated conceptual alignment research, meaning the use of advanced AI systems to help generate and refine conceptual ideas about how to align AI systems. The team is uncertain whether such automation can produce useful conceptual progress, since conceptual work is hard to verify and evaluate. They also recognise that tools and methods that make AI better at research-style reasoning could carry capability externalities, meaning they might speed up general AI capabilities as well as alignment progress. The team must decide whether the potential alignment benefits justify the uncertainty and the risk of externalities.
a_text: Pursue automated conceptual alignment research, and commit to shutting down any project that differentially accelerates capabilities.
b_text: Decline to pursue automated conceptual alignment research because of the risk that it spills over into general capability gains.
reason: Given the high importance, AGI companies will do it anyway, and there are safety-specific gains that are not general

context: A group of funders is preparing to offer grants in a set of new topic areas that have so far been described only at a high level. Some participants worry that announcing the grants before the funders have a detailed, concrete picture of what the areas involve could lead to poorly specified calls, mismatched applicants, or commitments that later need revision. Others believe the opportunity is time-sensitive and that public announcement would itself help attract proposals and clarify the areas through community response. The team must decide how to sequence announcement relative to the funders' own understanding of the areas.
a_text: Dismiss the concern about readiness and announce the grants publicly without further delay.
b_text: Delay the announcement until the funders have studied the concrete grant areas in more detail.
reason: Making the grants public would incentivize more people to think about scaling automated labor and would shape grantmakers' thinking

context: An AI safety research organisation focused on risks from deceptive or scheming AI systems must decide which research direction to prioritise as a core agenda. Two directions are under consideration. One is to build monitoring: tools that detect problematic or deceptive behaviour in model outputs and reasoning, an area where the team believes additional resources and scale would yield high returns. The other is to build a science of scheming: empirical studies of how misalignment emerges during reinforcement learning training of models. This direction rests on an expectation that scheming propensity and severity will increase as models become more capable and are trained with longer-horizon reinforcement learning. The team has current evidence about model behaviour and training, but the future trajectory of capabilities and training methods is uncertain. Only one direction can be made the main focus.
a_text: Prioritise a science of scheming that empirically studies how misalignment emerges in reinforcement learning, on the bet that scheming grows with capability.
b_text: Prioritise a monitoring agenda that builds tools to detect deceptive or problematic model behaviour, on the grounds that it offers high returns to scale.
reason: Monitoring has highly scalable data sources, a blue team vs. red team framing, and number-go-up-game structure

context: A team funds the staged expansion of a pipeline, and each further tranche of money requires a justification for scaling up. Two kinds of justification are available. One is commercial: evidence that the expanded capacity will be paid for. The other is empirical: evidence from the work itself that spending more is warranted. The team must decide what standard of evidence has to be met before more money is released.
a_text: Release further funding only once both parties pre-agree an empirical scaling condition, such as a plot of spending against a safety proxy.
b_text: Release further expansion funding only once customers sign long-term take-or-pay contracts that guarantee revenue regardless of the volume actually shipped.
reason: Funding should scale only when empirical evidence shows the pipeline converts money into safety, and the proxy must not be goodharted

context: A team is deploying a guardrail intended to prevent harmful or erroneous behaviour by an automated agent system. Before relying on it, they must decide what evidence will be accepted as showing the guardrail is good enough for deployment. The guardrail can be tested against a historical record of real failures that previously occurred, which shows whether it would have caught known problems. It can also be tested by having adversarial agents actively try to defeat it, which probes for weaknesses that have not yet appeared in practice. The team must choose the basis on which guardrail quality will be established.
a_text: Establish guardrail quality using both backtesting on past real failures and red-teaming with adversarial agents as the evidence.
b_text: Establish guardrail quality using only backtesting on past real failures, without any adversarial red-teaming as evidence.
reason: Agents can be reset and replayed under different rules, unlike human developers, so rules can be tested against real failures and adversarial trajectories to give evidence-based confidence.

context: A research team is considering systems that automate scientific research, including generating ideas, running experiments and writing up findings. They need a principled way to decide whether the output of such a system counts as real scientific progress rather than an artifact of the evaluation. Two concerns are salient: optimizing a proxy measure can produce apparent gains that do not reflect the target (Goodharting), and a system or its operators may deliberately overstate results. The team must settle on the basis for judging the system's output, knowing that purpose-built metrics are hard to design and that human judgment is costly and subjective but familiar from established scientific practice.
a_text: Judge the system's output by whether it passes human expert peer review, with humans involved in discovery, instead of relying on a designed metric.
b_text: Design metrics that faithfully measure the target and resist gaming, so that real progress can be separated from Goodharting and overclaiming.
reason: Models may strategically overclaim or manipulate results, so acceptance needs robust indicators.

context: A research team is planning how to assess the quality and trustworthiness of work produced by future automated AI safety researchers, meaning AI systems that carry out safety research with limited human oversight. Much of this work will be hard to verify directly, so the team must decide what kind of evidence to gather in advance to judge whether the output can be relied on. One approach centers on behavioral evidence from generalization studies, which examine how the AIs act on tasks whose answers can be checked and then extrapolate to tasks that cannot. The other approach centers on building a broad battery of indicators and metrics designed to resist gaming and overfitting, together with ways to study the adversarial strategies the AIs might use. The team knows that behavioral evidence can be misleading if the AIs are deliberately shaping their behavior, and that no single measure is guaranteed to stay informative once AIs optimize against it.
a_text: Rely mainly on behavioral evidence from generalization studies of AI performance on checkable tasks, and treat it as valid only after scheming has been ruled out.
b_text: Prepare a large set of gaming-resistant and overfitting-resistant metrics and indicators, along with procedures for understanding adversarial AI strategies.
reason: Evaluating thousands of proposals with limited time requires faithful, gaming-resistant indicators of real progress.

context: Researchers working today expect that AI systems will increasingly be able to carry out the execution of research projects, such as running experiments, analyses and implementation, in some fields more than in others. Within the next several years, the ability to execute may become cheap and abundant, while the ability to identify worthwhile questions and specify them clearly may remain scarce. Researchers must decide how to divide their current time between doing the hands-on work of projects and other activities, in a field where much of the execution is expected to be strongly automatable. There is uncertainty about how fast automation will arrive and how well it will handle execution, so the choice affects what skills and outputs researchers accumulate in the meantime.
a_text: Keep spending most research time directly executing projects yourself, including running experiments and analyses.
b_text: Spend a meaningful share of research time writing detailed research proposals rather than executing the projects.
reason: When execution becomes cheap, ideation becomes more important, especially for parallelizable research.

context: A research team is deciding where to direct effort in applying AI to its own scientific workflow. Current AI systems can reliably handle well-specified, repetitive engineering tasks such as running experiments, managing data and executing standard analysis steps. Their ability to generate novel ideas, judge which results matter and carry out open-ended research independently is much less proven and uncertain. The team must choose which kind of automation to emphasize given what current AI can do, knowing that capabilities may improve over time.
a_text: Prioritize automating the routine pipeline of experiments, data handling and analysis with current AI, and defer research automation.
b_text: Prioritize pipeline automation now, doubt that current AI can automate research itself, and build groundwork for that later.
reason: Many safety pipelines can be automated today with direct benefit, while current capabilities probably don't suffice for research automation.

context: A research team is planning how to use AI systems for safety work, such as alignment and risk-reduction research, as AI capabilities advance. At any given time, the team must decide which generation of AI systems to rely on for a given safety task. Earlier systems are available now and can provide some meaningful help, but they are less capable and may be less reliable. Later successor systems are expected to be more capable, though they would arrive later and may carry greater risks if they are less well understood or less trustworthy. The team must choose a timing policy for deploying AI on safety tasks.
a_text: Use the earliest AI systems that can meaningfully help with a given safety task, and start using them as soon as they are available.
b_text: Delay AI assistance on a given safety task until more capable successor systems are available, and rely on those instead.
reason: Otherwise there is a large opportunity cost in safety progress, and successor systems are less safe because earlier safety advances weren't used.

context: A research team is building a post-training pipeline for reasoning that combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on curated data followed by reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards. They want to apply it to several open-weight base model families of comparable size, so that conclusions are not tied to a single family. RL is far more compute-intensive and engineering-heavy than SFT, and it must be tuned separately for each family's tokenizer, context handling and training stability. The team has a fixed compute budget and must decide how widely to apply the RL stage across the families they study.
a_text: Run RL on a single model family and use SFT alone for all the other families.
b_text: Run the full SFT-then-RL pipeline on every open-weight model family under study.
reason: SFT gives the dominant gain, and full RL on every family would raise cost and add per-model tuning confounds.

context: A research team is building a pipeline that uses a frontier language model as a teacher to generate rationales, which will then be used to train a smaller model. They must choose which frontier model serves as the teacher. The candidates are several recent frontier models from different providers, including an earlier-generation model and a newer-generation model from the same family. The choice affects the quality and style of the generated rationales and the cost of producing them at scale. The team must commit to one teacher before generating the full set of rationales.
a_text: Use the newer-generation model from the family as the teacher for rationale generation.
b_text: Use the earlier-generation model from the family as the teacher for rationale generation.
reason: It had the best schema faithfulness and rubric score calibration. Gemini 3.1 Pro gave concise rationales and low benign scores, Claude had calibration inconsistencies, and GPT-5.4 gave high benign scores.

context: A research team trained language models with supervised fine-tuning and then added a reinforcement learning stage. Evaluation across several task families showed that the reinforcement learning stage improved performance only slightly over the supervised baseline, and the improvement varied considerably between tasks. Some tasks, such as open-ended generation scored by a judge model for semantic correctness, showed visible gains, while structured tasks such as classification and function calling showed little or no change. The team had to decide how to explain these small and uneven gains.
a_text: Explain the uneven gains by task type, crediting reinforcement learning with helping mainly open-ended generative tasks that a judge can reward and adding little to structured tasks.
b_text: Explain the small gains by the role of the stage, treating reinforcement learning as a refinement step on top of supervised training instead of the main source of capability.
reason: SFT gives the large gains, and RL slightly reduces pAUROC@20 on some splits while improving the aggregate.

context: A research team trained models on mixtures of behavioral data of increasing breadth and measured how a targeted behavior changed as the mixture widened. The measured effect was non-monotonic: adding more diverse data did not produce steady gains or steady reductions, and one additional synthetic data source gave no benefit at all. The team had to decide how to interpret this pattern and what general statement to make about the role of training mixtures. One reading treats breadth of behavioral coverage as the main driver of the outcome. Another reading treats the pattern as arising from how examples in a mixture interact with one another, rather than from the properties of each example alone.
a_text: State that examples interact within a mixture, so diluting a subset with benign data of the same kind can strengthen its effect and data cannot be judged in isolation.
b_text: State that broader behavioral coverage is the key factor, despite the non-monotonic gains and the lack of benefit from the extra synthetic source.
reason: Gains were limited when adding Gloom but significant with Bash and coding sabotage data.

context: A research team is evaluating a trained detector for scheming behavior in AI agents and needs to compare it against prompted frontier language models used as baselines. Fairness depends on how those baselines are configured, since results can vary considerably with the prompt used. The team can either rely on an existing, previously published prompt for scheming detection, or explore several prompt designs, including a detailed specification of what counts as scheming, and select among them based on performance. The choice affects how strong the baselines are and how credible the comparison is.
a_text: Use a single existing scheming-detection prompt taken from previously published work for the baselines without further variation.
b_text: Test several prompt variants for the baselines and report the best-performing one, which is a detailed full specification of scheming.
reason: The specification prompt performed best on aggregate pAUROC@20 over the OOD datasets.

context: A research team is training a smaller language model, Qwen3-8B, by distilling data from a teacher model. The standard setup uses a much larger frontier model to generate the teacher outputs, which is costly and depends on an external system. The team considers whether the 8B model itself could generate the teacher data for its own training, removing the need for a frontier model. Self-generation would be cheaper and simpler, but the model's outputs might be weaker or less informative than a frontier model's, which could limit the gains from training.
a_text: Use the 8B model as its own teacher and drop the frontier model for generating data.
b_text: Keep the frontier model as the teacher and drop self-generation by the 8B model.
reason: Self-generation yielded only 384 filtered examples, too few to train a competitive monitor.

context: A research team is designing a reinforcement learning reward for a model that must assess items against labels that come with graded severity or score bands, while the core task is deciding whether a target condition is present. Two reward families are available. One uses only the binary ground-truth label, optimizing calibration of predicted probabilities and the ranking of positive items above negative ones. The other also uses the ordinal grading, so that the reward reflects how severe an item is and whether its score band is preserved. The ordinal option carries more information from the annotations but adds design complexity and extra assumptions about how bands should be weighted. The binary option is simpler and discards severity information. The team must choose which reward design to use for training.
a_text: Use a reward that combines binary detection with preservation of ordinal score bands so that severity is reflected in training.
b_text: Use a deliberately simple reward built only from binary labels, combining calibration and pairwise ranking without any severity information.
reason: The goal was to test whether lightweight RL can improve action-only monitoring beyond supervised distillation.

context: A research team is distilling teacher-written rationales into a student model for detecting scheming behaviour in chain-of-thought reasoning, using a benchmark of reasoning traces labelled as scheming or benign. They use an automated judge to score the quality of each teacher rationale. The judge assigns low scores to most of the rationales for scheming samples, so the rationales cannot all be accepted as they are. The team must decide how to decide which teacher rationales to trust, given that the judge's absolute scores appear poorly calibrated for the scheming class.
a_text: Corrupt each rationale's logic on purpose and keep only the rationales that the judge scores clearly above their corrupted versions.
